chapters.title: Africa
chapters.story: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco. For most of our history, every human alive lived on this one continent.

chapters.title: White Sands · North America
chapters.story: Footprints pressed into a lakeshore in New Mexico, dated by seeds trapped in the layers. People were in the Americas during the last glacial maximum, far earlier than once thought.

chapters.title: Southwest Asia · and beyond
chapters.story: At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers raised carved stone pillars before they farmed. Within a few thousand years, wheat, barley, sheep and goats were domesticated across the Fertile Crescent.

chapters.title: Uruk · Mesopotamia
chapters.story: The first city. Tens of thousands of people, monumental temples, and clay tablets pressed with the earliest writing, invented to keep accounts.

chapters.title: Giza · Egypt
chapters.story: The Great Pyramid, 2.3 million blocks aligned to the cardinal directions within a twentieth of a degree. It stayed the tallest human structure for 3,800 years.

chapters.title: Mohenjo-daro · Indus Valley
chapters.story: A planned city on a grid, with covered drains, private bathrooms and a great bath, built by a civilization whose script we still cannot read.

chapters.title: East & Central Asia
chapters.story: Han China and Rome never met, but silk, glass, horses and ideas crossed the deserts and mountains between them along routes later called the Silk Road.

chapters.title: Central Mexico
chapters.story: Teotihuacan held perhaps 125,000 people, among the largest cities on Earth, laid out along an avenue aimed at the Pyramid of the Moon.

chapters.title: Mississippi Valley · North America
chapters.story: Cahokia, across the river from modern St. Louis, was a city of earthen mounds and plazas larger than London at the time.

chapters.title: Polynesia · the Pacific
chapters.story: Navigators reading stars, swells and birds settled the last habitable places on Earth, from Hawai'i to Aotearoa to Rapa Nui, across a third of the planet's surface.

chapters.title: Northern China · Ming era
chapters.story: Beijing's Forbidden City rose in 1420. The Great Wall took its familiar stone form. Zheng He's treasure fleets sailed as far as East Africa.

chapters.title: Machu Picchu · the Andes
chapters.story: An Inca estate on a ridge 2,430 m up, built without mortar, wheels or iron, linked to an empire by 40,000 km of road.

chapters.title: Timbuktu · West Africa
chapters.story: A university city at the edge of the Sahara, where caravans traded salt for gold and scholars copied hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.

chapters.title: Atlantic Ocean · the Caribbean
chapters.story: Columbus reached the Bahamas. The hemispheres were joined; crops, animals, diseases and people began to move in both directions, remaking every society they touched.

chapters.title: Philadelphia · North America
chapters.story: A declaration that governments derive their powers from the consent of the governed, written in a rented room and read aloud in the yard of the State House.

chapters.title: Ironbridge · Britain
chapters.story: The first bridge cast entirely from iron spanned the Severn in 1779. Coal, iron and steam were about to change how everything was made.

chapters.title: Lower Manhattan · New York
chapters.story: On 4 September 1882 the Pearl Street station lit 400 lamps in a few blocks of Manhattan. Night, for the first time, could be switched off.

chapters.title: One shared planet
chapters.story: Eight billion people. The lights we leave on at night trace where we live, and the dark places remind us how much of the planet is still not ours.
